problem: Zero-shot semantic navigation methods lack a global structured semantic memory and rely on local observations with greedy/heuristic frontier search, causing myopic exploration, redundant backtracking and accumulated errors from misaligned foundation-model priors, especially in long-distance episodes. Existing hierarchical 3D scene graphs are built offline assuming full observability.
motivation: Long-horizon decision-making needs a compact structured state space with multi-granular semantic abstraction that can be built online under partial observation. Foundation-model priors can misalign with the actual scene, so the agent needs observation feedback to correct its belief, and needs explicit lookahead to avoid greedy behavior.
key_idea: Incrementally build an online Object-Zone-Region hierarchical 3D scene graph (GVD + spectral clustering) and use it as both a belief state (LLM prior x frontier-information-gain evidence) and a lightweight simulator for POUCT rollouts to choose macro-actions with long-term expected return.
insight: Ablations on HM3Dv2 show every component contributes: removing rollouts (H=0) drops SPL from 39.5 to 35.9, removing evidence drops SR to 76.0 and removing the zone level to 79.5/38.2. The level-horizon ablation shows an optimal planning horizon: too large H accumulates HSG-simulator model bias, and the finer L=2 hierarchy prefers a shorter horizon than L=1. Gains are largest on long-distance episodes (>10 m), which supports the claim that the benefit comes from global memory plus lookahead.
method: Online object mapping: YOLOE open-vocabulary segmentation projected to 3D with depth and pose, fused into object nodes (ConceptGraphs-style), plus an occupancy map.
Object-level Voronoi partition: a generalized Voronoi diagram on the occupancy map assigns explored cells to the nearest object, giving an object adjacency graph.

Zone/Region construction: spectral clustering on adjacency edges weighted by spatial proximity times semantic similarity, applied bottom-up (objects to zones to regions); incremental update every N steps with local edge recomputation and re-clustering.
Node semantic descriptions: VLM captions of keyframes for zones, LLM summaries for regions, accumulated labels for objects; also used for the stop decision (VLM check in TextInstanceNav).

Hierarchical belief: region belief = Norm(LLM semantic prior x exploration evidence), where evidence is the fraction of frontier information gain above a target-size-dependent threshold; virtual unexplored region/zone nodes.

HSG simulator + POUCT: simulator with found/not_found observations and reward R_succ minus lambda times shortest-path movement cost; POUCT with horizon H estimates Q of visit(region) then visit(zone) macro-actions.
Local planner: frontiers of the selected region/zone ordered by an ATSP tour (FUEL), paths by Fast Marching Method, discretized into low-level actions.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-8B (frozen, as VLM and LLM) + YOLOE (frozen) + POUCT planner
setting.action_space: low-level discrete move_forward/turn_left/turn_right/stop, via macro-actions visit(region/zone) and frontier tours
setting.privileged: none (assumes posed RGB-D, i.e. ground-truth pose/odometry)

numbers_note: Split names are not stated explicitly in the paper; 'val' is assumed for standard ObjectNav validation sets. Long-distance results (>10 m subset) are only shown in a figure and supplementary material, not in the text (only averages +9.4% SR / +5.0% SPL are stated).
results: Across four ObjectNav datasets the method beats the strong training-free baseline ApexNav by an average of 5.4% SR and 2.3% SPL (e.g., HM3Dv2 80.1/39.5 vs 76.2/38.0; HSSD 69.9/36.4 vs 61.1/31.5). On TextInstanceNav it reaches 38.1 SR / 16.0 SPL vs UniGoal's 20.2/11.4, and on long-distance episodes (>10 m) it improves SR and SPL by 9.4% and 5.0% on average.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation and assumes posed RGB-D; real-world localization errors may hurt object fusion and mapping.
VLM/LLM inference causes substantial latency, preventing real-time execution.
HSG simulator is an approximation of the real environment, so large planning horizons accumulate model bias.
